plain_english:
It causes endless problems when you try to hide your true feelings. You never let anyone see who you really are. Instead, like many people, you live a fake life to impress others. This constant self-monitoring becomes torture. You're always afraid someone will catch you acting out of character. We can never relax if we think everyone is judging our worth. Many things happen that strip away our disguise, no matter how hard we fight to keep it. Even if you succeed at fooling everyone, life isn't happy or safe when you always have to wear a mask.

But there's real joy in honest simplicity. It's beautiful on its own and hides nothing. Still, this open life does risk being looked down on. Some people scorn whatever they get close to. But virtue can't become contemptible when people see it clearly. It's better to be mocked for your simplicity than to carry the burden of endless pretending.

We need balance here, though. There's a big difference between living simply and living carelessly.
original_excerpt: It also proves a fertile source of troubles if you take pains to conceal your feelings and never show yourself to any one undisguised, but, as many men do, live an artificial life, in order to impose upon others: for the constant watching of himself becomes a torment to a man, and he dreads being caught doing something at variance with his usual habits, and, indeed, we never can be at our ease if we imagine that every one who looks at us is weighing our real value: for many things occur which strip people of their disguise, however reluctantly they may part with it, and even if all this trouble about oneself is successful, still life is neither happy nor safe when one always has to wear a mask. But what pleasure there is in that honest straight-forwardness which is its own ornament, and which conceals no part of its character! Yet even this life, which hides nothing from any one runs some risk of being despised; for there are people who disdain whatever they come close to: but there is no danger of virtue's becoming contemptible when she is brought near our eyes, and it is better to be scorned for one's simplicity than to bear the burden of unceasing hypocrisy. Still, we must observe moderation in this matter, for there is a great difference between living simply and living slovenly.

plain_english: We should spend plenty of time alone with ourselves. Being around people who are different from us disrupts our peace. It stirs up emotions that were calm and reopens old wounds that haven't fully healed yet. But we need to balance solitude with being around others. We should alternate between time alone and time in crowds. Solitude will make us appreciate other people. Crowds will make us appreciate being alone. Each one cures what the other causes: solitude heals us when we're tired of people, and people heal us when we're tired of being alone.
original_excerpt: Moreover, we ought to retire a great deal into ourselves: for association with persons unlike ourselves upsets all that we had arranged, rouses the passions which were at rest, and rubs into a sore any weak or imperfectly healed place in our minds. Nevertheless we ought to mix up these two things, and to pass our lives alternately in solitude and among throngs of people; for the former will make us long for the society of mankind, the latter for that of ourselves, and the one will counteract the other: solitude will cure us when we are sick of crowds, and crowds will cure us when we are sick of solitude.

plain_english: We shouldn't always keep our minds at full intensity. Sometimes we need to relax and have fun. Socrates wasn't embarrassed to play with children. Cato would unwind with wine after exhausting himself on government business. Scipio would dance to music with his battle-hardened body — not with the weak, shuffling steps that are fashionable today (we sway when we walk with less strength than women), but with the bold, athletic dancing that men used to do at parties and festivals. He saw nothing wrong with his enemies seeing him dance like this. Our minds need to relax. They come back stronger and sharper after rest. You can't force crops from rich soil forever — endless heavy harvests will drain the land's fertility. The same thing happens to our mental sharpness if we work without stopping. But our minds recover their strength after a short break. Constant work creates a kind of dullness and sluggishness.
original_excerpt: Neither ought we always to keep the mind strained to the same pitch, but it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement. Socrates did not blush to play with little boys, Cato used to refresh his mind with wine after he had wearied it with application to affairs of state, and Scipio would move his triumphal and soldierly limbs to the sound of music, not with a feeble and halting gait, as is the fashion now-a-days, when we sway in our very walk with more than womanly weakness, but dancing as men were wont in the days of old on sportive and festal occasions, with manly bounds, thinking it no harm to be seen so doing even by their enemies. Men's minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest. We must not force crops from rich fields, for an unbroken course of heavy crops will soon exhaust their fertility, and so also the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour, but they will recover their strength after a short period of rest and relief: for continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness.

plain_english:
People wouldn't be so drawn to games and entertainment if these things didn't naturally appeal to us. But if you indulge in them constantly, your mind loses all its seriousness and strength. Sleep is also necessary to refresh us. But if you sleep for days and nights straight, it becomes death. There's a big difference between loosening your grip on something and completely letting it go.

The founders of our laws created festivals so people would be publicly encouraged to be cheerful. They thought it was necessary to mix our work with fun. As I said before, some great men used to give themselves a certain number of holidays each month. Others divided every day into playtime and work time.

I remember that great speaker Asinius Pollio wouldn't handle any business after the tenth hour. He wouldn't even read letters after that time, afraid some new problem might come up. Instead, he used those two hours to shake off the tiredness he had built up during the whole day. Some people rest in the middle of the day and save light tasks for the afternoon. Our ancestors also forbade any new business to be brought up in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers divide their watch duties. And those who have just returned from active service are allowed to sleep through the entire night undisturbed.
original_excerpt: Men would not be so eager for this, if play and amusement did not possess natural attractions for them, although constant indulgence in them takes away all gravity and all strength from the mind: for sleep, also, is necessary for our refreshment, yet if you prolong it for days and nights together it will become death. There is a great difference between slackening your hold of a thing and letting it go. The founders of our laws appointed festivals, in order that men might be publicly encouraged to be cheerful, and they thought it necessary to vary our labours with amusements, and, as I said before, some great men have been wont to give themselves a certain number of holidays in every month, and some divided every day into play-time and work-time. Thus, I remember that great orator Asinius Pollio would not attend to any business after the tenth hour: he would not even read letters after that time for fear some new trouble should arise, but in those two hours used to get rid of the weariness which he had contracted during the whole day. Some rest in the middle of the day, and reserve some light occupation for the afternoon. Our ancestors, too, forbade any new motion to be made in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers divide their watches, and those who have just returned from active service are allowed to sleep the whole night undisturbed.

plain_english: We need to give our minds a break now and then. Rest acts like food for the mind — it restores our strength. It's also good to take walks outside. Fresh air and a cool breeze lift our spirits and refresh us. Sometimes we gain strength by taking a carriage ride, traveling, changing scenery, or sharing meals with friends and drinking more wine than usual. At times we should even drink to the point of being drunk — not to drown ourselves, but just to take a dip in wine. Wine washes away our troubles and pulls them up from deep in our minds. It works as medicine for sorrow, just like it does for some diseases. The god who invented wine is called Liber — not because wine loosens our tongues, but because it frees our minds from worry. It liberates us, gives us life, and makes us bolder in everything we try. But moderation is healthy in both freedom and wine. People say that Solon and Arcesilaus drank heavily. Cato gets criticized for being a drunk. But anyone who throws that accusation at him will find it easier to turn their insult into praise than to prove Cato did anything wrong. Still, we shouldn't do this often. We don't want our minds to pick up bad habits. But sometimes we should force ourselves to be playful and honest, and throw off our dull seriousness for a while.
original_excerpt: We must humour our minds and grant them rest from time to time, which acts upon them like food, and restores their strength. It does good also to take walks out of doors, that our spirits may be raised and refreshed by the open air and fresh breeze: sometimes we gain strength by driving in a carriage, by travel, by change of air, or by social meals and a more generous allowance of wine: at times we ought to drink even to intoxication, not so as to drown, but merely to dip ourselves in wine: for wine washes away troubles and dislodges them from the depths of the mind, and acts as a remedy to sorrow as it does to some diseases. The inventor of wine is called Liber, not from the licence which he gives to our tongues, but because he liberates the mind from the bondage of cares, and emancipates it, animates it, and renders it more daring in all that it attempts. Yet moderation is wholesome both in freedom and in wine. It is believed that Solon and Arcesilaus used to drink deep. Cato is reproached with drunkenness: but whoever casts this in his teeth will find it easier to turn his reproach into a commendation than to prove that Cato did anything wrong: however, we ought not to do it often, for fear the mind should contract evil habits, though it ought sometimes to be forced into frolic and frankness, and to cast off dull sobriety for a while.

plain_english: If we believe the Greek poet, "it's sometimes pleasant to be mad." Plato could never write poetry when he was sober. And if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever been without a touch of madness. The mind can't use grand language — the kind that rises above ordinary speech — unless it gets excited. When it pushes aside the dull habits of everyday life and rises up, filled with sacred fire, only then can it sing a song too beautiful for human lips. As long as the mind stays calm and controlled, it can't reach any real brilliance. It must break away from the safe path and whip itself into a frenzy, until it bites through its restraints and carries its rider to heights it would be too scared to climb alone.
original_excerpt: If we believe the Greek poet, "it is sometimes pleasant to be mad"; again, Plato always knocked in vain at the door of poetry when he was sober; or, if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever been without a touch of insanity. The mind cannot use lofty language, above that of the common herd, unless it be excited. When it has spurned aside the commonplace environments of custom, and rises sublime, instinct with sacred fire, then alone can it chant a song too grand for mortal lips: as long as it continues to dwell within itself it cannot rise to any pitch of splendour: it must break away from the beaten track, and lash itself to frenzy, till it gnaws the curb and rushes away bearing up its rider to heights whither it would fear to climb when alone.

plain_english: I've now told you, my dear Serenus, what can protect peace of mind, what can restore it when we lose it, and what can stop the vices that quietly eat away at it. But understand this: none of these methods is strong enough to help us keep such a fragile blessing. We have to watch over our wavering minds with intense and constant care.
original_excerpt: I have now, my beloved Serenus, given you an account of what things can preserve peace of mind, what things can restore it to us, what can arrest the vices which secretly undermine it: yet be assured, that none of these is strong enough to enable us to retain so fleeting a blessing, unless we watch over our vacillating mind with intense and unremitting care.
